chapters.title: US Dollar
chapters.teaser: Hot data, soft dollar: import prices +1.1% and factory output +0.7% both beat, and the dollar fell anyway — DXY 101.61 (-0.42%), its first weekly loss in five. Reuters put the October hold at ~85%.
chapters.meaning: What changed: Friday delivered the week's third hot inflation print — import prices rose 1.1% in September vs ~0.8% expected, up 8.1% from a year ago, the biggest yearly jump since July 2022; export prices jumped 2.2%. Factory output beat too (+0.7% vs +0.4%, the sixth straight monthly gain). And the dollar fell anyway: DXY closed 101.61 (-0.42%), its first weekly loss in five. The 10-year touched 5.125% on the data, then settled ~5.09% — the bond market read the hot prints and still wouldn't price an October hike. Reuters' Friday wire put October hold at ~85%, up from ~70% Thursday night. The Treasury's books also landed: September's deficit came in at -$26.9B vs -$34.7B expected (narrower = better), though FY2026's $1.992T is the largest deficit in five years; foreign demand for US assets stayed strong (TIC +$199.8B vs $75.2B fcst). Thread: this morning the story was Warsh's 'I don't prejudge meetings' — his last word before Saturday's blackout — with October ~30% hike, priced as a hold. What it means: confirms, and sharpens. The October question is settled: the market treats October 27-28 as a hold and has moved the debate to December. The four-beat read on import prices: (1) it's what America pays for foreign goods — up 1.1% in a single month; (2) the beat vs ~0.8% makes three hot inflation prints in three days (CPI 3.7%, PPI 1.3%, now this); (3) +8.1% from a year ago means import inflation is running at a four-year high — tariffs and energy feeding straight through; (4) for the dollar the chain is: more inflation pressure → the Fed stays hawkish → December hike odds rise → but October is locked, so the dollar reads it as 'higher later, not now' and fades into the weekend.
chapters.fx: What to watch: blackout starts Saturday — no Fed voices until the meeting. Goolsbee on Bloomberg TV 6pm ET tonight is the last scheduled speaker. Weekend risk is headline-driven: Iran/Hormuz, oil. Next week: China Q3 GDP, NZ Q3 CPI, US housing starts (Tue), Canada CPI (Tue), then FOMC Oct 27-28.

chapters.title: Euro
chapters.teaser: The euro's two-day rebound ran on the dollar's weakness, not its own strength — EUR/USD ~1.1255-1.1259 (+0.33%), up from Wednesday's 17-month low of 1.1113. Correction: the ECB's Oct 29 meeting is NOT priced as a hike; December is 100%.
chapters.meaning: What changed: EUR/USD added ~0.3% to ~1.1255-1.1259, now ~1.4% off Wednesday's 17-month low (1.1113) — the pair's first weekly gain in over a month. The driver is still the dollar fade: the euro gained less than sterling or the Aussie, and EUR/GBP fell 0.34% to 0.8421. Correction to this morning's read: the October 29 ECB meeting is not priced as a hike. Friday's Reuters bond-market report says traders see no October move; a December hike is priced at 100%, with at least one more by April. September's 3.8% CPI (a three-year high, energy +18.9%) stands — the market just believes the ECB waits for December. Thread: morning — EUR/USD closed +0.56% at ~1.1218, the biggest daily gain in ~2 months, on the dollar fade not euro strength; final CPI confirmed 3.8%. What it means: confirms the morning thesis and corrects the policy read. The euro's rebound is borrowed momentum — it works only while US yields keep falling. The four-beat read on the ECB pricing: (1) no October hike expected — the market gives the meeting no chance; (2) that replaces this morning's 'live meeting' wording, which was wrong; (3) December at 100% means the ECB's next move is a question of when in winter, not whether — 3.8% inflation with energy +18.9% is far above the 2% target; (4) for the euro: a December ECB hike against a Fed on hold narrows the 170bp US-German yield gap that has been crushing it — the euro's only self-powered tailwind, and it starts in December.
chapters.fx: What to watch: French fiscal headlines (OAT-Bund 135.2bp); ECB speakers next week; the US 10Y–Bund spread (170bp) — a 10Y move toward 5.00% gives the euro room, a return to 5.20%+ kills the rebound.
numbers: ECB: no Oct hike priced; Dec 100%, ≥1 more by April

scenarios.base: Dollar-fade rebound extends while the 10Y stays under 5.10%; 1.1277 caps.
scenarios.bear: Hot weekend headline or 10Y back over 5.20% — retest of 1.12.

chapters.title: British Pound
chapters.teaser: Sterling was the majors' best performer — GBP/USD +0.60% to 1.3353, +0.92% on the week — riding Thursday's GDP beat and the dollar fade. Bailey's dovish-leaning line didn't dent it.
chapters.meaning: What changed: GBP/USD closed +0.60% at 1.3353 — its best day of the week, +0.92% on the week — and outperformed the euro (EUR/GBP fell to 0.8421). The fuel was Thursday's GDP beat (+0.1% vs -0.1% fcst) repricing the November 5 BoE meeting, plus the broad dollar fade. Bailey's overnight remarks — second-round effects 'quite subdued', August's 3.1% CPI 'enormously frustrating' — leaned dovish on the 2027 path but left November untouched, and the market chose the GDP read over Bailey's caution. Thread: morning — Bailey spoke overnight (~2am CT) with a dovish lean on 2027; the Nov 5 hike case stood on the GDP beat. What it means: confirms. Sterling's bid is the week's cleanest: growth beat + priced November hike + dollar fade, all pointing the same way. Four beats on the GDP print: (1) the UK economy grew 0.1% in August; (2) the beat vs -0.1% expected is a small number with a big signal — services drove a 3M/3M pickup; (3) 2.1% y/y is the strongest since Aug 2022 — the UK is growing while its inflation runs 3.1%, which is why a November hike is priced; (4) for the pound: growth that justifies the hike it's priced for → the currency holds its bid while the Fed debates.
chapters.fx: What to watch: UK jobs and CPI next week — a hot CPI cements November; a soft one reopens Bailey's dovish 2027 read. Weekend risk is dollar-side.

chapters.title: Japanese Yen
chapters.teaser: The yen lagged the dollar selloff — USD/JPY 157.79-157.89 (-0.12%) while the euro and pound gained three to five times more. Ueda leaned hawkish on inflation-overshoot risks, but the ~216bp US-Japan yield gap still rules.
chapters.meaning: What changed: USD/JPY closed ~157.8-157.9, down just 0.12% — the smallest gain of any major against the dollar (euro +0.34%, sterling +0.69%, kiwi +0.65%). Ueda used Friday to lean hawkish, flagging inflation-overshoot risks into the Oct 29-30 BoJ meeting, and Japanese officials warned on the currency. But the US-Japan 10-year gap sits near 216bp — as long as it stays this wide, money earns far more in dollars, and the yen can't rally on its own. Thread: morning — USD/JPY faded to 157.92 (-0.34%) with the 10-year; a US Treasury undersecretary spoke on the yen in Bangkok. What it means: confirms, with a warning label. The yen is the laggard of the dollar fade — it needs the US 10-year to fall, not just the dollar. Four beats on the yield gap: (1) the US 10-year pays ~5.09%, Japan's ~2.93% — a ~216bp gap; (2) that gap is the price of holding yen instead of dollars; (3) it's why Ueda's hawkish lean barely moved the pair — words don't close a 216bp gap, rate moves do; (4) for the yen: the BoJ's Oct 29-30 meeting is the next chance to narrow it — a hawkish surprise there is the yen's only self-powered catalyst. Intervention chatter sits at 160.
chapters.fx: What to watch: BoJ Oct 29-30 — Ueda's overshoot-risk language is the setup; US 10Y direction; 160 as the intervention line.

chapters.title: Swiss Franc
chapters.teaser: USD/CHF 0.8228 (-0.48%) — the franc added to Thursday's haven bid as oil surged, +1.4% in two sessions. No new Swiss driver; quiet.
chapters.meaning: What changed: nothing Swiss — the franc's second straight up-day is the dollar fade plus haven flow as oil jumped back over $100. USD/CHF closed 0.8228 (-0.48%), +1.4% for the franc in two sessions. Thread: Thursday's +0.57% was the haven bid; Schlegel spoke with no new signal and Swiss PPI stayed soft (+0.3%), keeping December cut risk on the table. What it means: the franc is doing its job — rising when risk wobbles — without any help from the SNB. A December cut is still the base case if data stays soft; the haven bid is the offset.

chapters.title: Australian Dollar
chapters.teaser: The risk bid came back — AUD/USD +0.5-0.6% to ~0.6946-0.6960 — as Asia rebounded from Thursday's AI rout. The domestic texture is still Thursday's soft jobs print.
chapters.meaning: What changed: AUD/USD closed ~0.6946-0.6960 (+0.35-0.6%), riding the broad dollar fade and a risk-on turn — Asia bounced (Kospi +2.8%, Nikkei +1.8%) after Thursday's AI-led rout. No new Australian data; the domestic story is still Thursday's soft jobs report (-39.3K vs +19.6K fcst, unemployment 4.7%, a five-year high), which questions the RBA's November thinking after the Sep 29 hike to 4.60%. Thread: morning — the positioning lens flipped: hedge funds are net LONG AUD, which broke the squeeze story. What it means: confirms the contrarian read. The Aussie rallied on risk, not on Australia — and with funds already long (79th percentile), this is exactly the setup where a risk wobble unwinds fast. Four beats on the positioning flip: (1) hedge funds hold net long AUD; (2) that broke this week's squeeze thesis — you can't squeeze shorts that aren't there; (3) under the contrarian rule, stretched longs mean the pain trade is down, not up; (4) for the Aussie: rallies into long positioning are rented, not owned — watch whether risk holds over the weekend.
chapters.fx: What to watch: weekend risk tone; RBA speakers; China Q3 GDP next week — the Aussie's real fundamentals.

chapters.title: Canadian Dollar
chapters.teaser: Two-way Canadian data, one clear tailwind: housing starts beat (248,896 vs 234K), foreigners dumped a record C$17.3B of Canadian securities, and WTI's jump back over $100 did the heavy lifting — USD/CAD -0.3% to 1.4147.
chapters.meaning: What changed: Canada printed in both directions. Housing starts beat — 248,896 SAAR vs 234K expected (+2.8% m/m), though actual starts are still down 11% y/y and CMHC flags underbuilding risk. Foreign securities was the big miss: nonresidents sold a net C$17.31B in August vs +C$23.59B expected — the first monthly divestment of 2026, led by a record C$17.5B cut in federal government debt. And oil did the lifting: WTI back above $100 is a terms-of-trade gift for the loonie. USD/CAD closed -0.3% at 1.4147. Thread: morning — Macklem leaned hawkish overnight ('the longer it goes, the harder it is to look through' energy prices), putting the Oct 28 hike option back on the table. What it means: confirms and strengthens. Macklem's hawkish lean plus $100 oil is the BoC's hiking fuel — the energy inflation the governor says he can't 'look through' is now at his doorstep. Four beats on the foreign-securities miss: (1) foreigners sold C$17.3B of Canadian securities in August; (2) a huge miss vs +C$23.6B expected — the first net selling of 2026; (3) the selling targeted federal government debt (a record C$17.5B cut) — foreigners stepping back from Canada's sovereign paper, a quiet confidence vote; (4) for the loonie: foreign selling of Canadian assets is a headwind, but it's August data — the market cares more about October's oil and the Oct 28 BoC.
chapters.fx: What to watch: Canada CPI Tuesday — the number that decides whether Macklem's hawkish lean becomes a hike; oil over the weekend.

chapters.title: New Zealand Dollar
chapters.teaser: The kiwi led the commodity bloc — NZD/USD +0.65% to 0.5658, a two-week high and its first weekly gain since August — on the dollar fade plus Thursday's red-hot 56.5 manufacturing PMI.
chapters.meaning: What changed: NZD/USD closed ~0.5658 (+0.65%), the strongest of the majors on the day, extending Thursday's bounce off the 18-month low (0.5565). The pair is on track for its first weekly advance since mid-August. The domestic fuel was Thursday's BNZ manufacturing PMI at 56.5 — the strongest since 2021, 15th straight month of expansion — feeding the RBNZ-hike side of the Oct 28 two-way bet; flat food prices fed the hold side. Thread: morning — two-way data for the two-way bet: PMI 56.5 vs flat food prices into the Oct 28 RBNZ. What it means: confirms. The kiwi's rally is still mostly the dollar fade, but the PMI gives the RBNZ-hike camp real ammunition. Four beats on the PMI: (1) New Zealand factory activity scored 56.5 in September; (2) a beat vs 53.1 prior — above 50 means expanding, and 56.5 is the strongest since 2021; (3) 15 straight months of expansion with employment back growing — a real industrial upswing, not a blip; (4) for the kiwi: strong factories + the RBNZ's Conway saying a hike is the most likely outcome = the market prices October 28 as a live hike — but NZ Q3 CPI next week is the number that confirms or kills it.
chapters.fx: What to watch: NZ Q3 CPI next week — the decider for Oct 28; RBNZ speakers.

scenarios.bull: Hot NZ CPI — October hike priced, test 0.57+.

chapters.title: Oil
chapters.teaser: Escalation won the day: Ukraine's renewed strikes on Russian refineries sent front-month WTI +2.8% to $100.71 — its first close over $100 in a month — and Dec Brent +3.2% to $109.28. The Brent-WTI spread sits near $10.7, a wide geopolitical premium.
chapters.meaning: What changed: Friday's surge came from Ukraine, not Hormuz — renewed strikes on Russian refineries, with the White House reportedly pressuring Kyiv to stop via Starshield limits (Reuters Oct 15 exclusive; a senior US official denied the president personally made the request). Front-month (Nov) WTI jumped 2.8% to $100.71, the first close above $100 in a month; Dec Brent rose 3.2% to $109.28; even Dec WTI added 2.2% to $98.59. The pullbacks are lined up: the IEA agreed to release the remaining 100M barrels of emergency reserves (incl. ~20M diesel), the US is weighing easing shadow-fleet tanker sanctions, and Vitol notes Hormuz fuel-oil flows are still down ≥800k tons/month vs February. Thread: morning — escalation and release pulled opposite ways: CENTCOM confirmed an Iranian projectile sank a Hormuz container ship while the IEA readied diesel. What it means: the morning's two-way pull is now a one-way tape with a ceiling. Four beats on the $100 print: (1) WTI closed above $100 for the first time in a month; (2) the +2.8% day came from a supply shock (refinery strikes), not demand; (3) $100+ oil with US gasoline above $4 for a record 158 straight days means demand destruction is already biting — consumers drive less, which caps how far this runs; (4) for FX: $100 oil is a tailwind for CAD and a headwind for JPY (Japan imports nearly all its energy) — and the Brent-WTI spread near $10.7 says the market prices this as geopolitical, not fundamental.
chapters.fx: What to watch: weekend refinery-strike headlines; whether Kyiv heeds the Starshield pressure; Hormuz flow data (Kpler: 68% of baseline).

chapters.title: Gold
chapters.teaser: The anti-dollar bid held but didn't extend — spot ~$4,167-4,182, up slightly on the day, still capped below $4,200. Falling yields helped; hot US data and a priced December hike kept the ceiling on.
chapters.meaning: What changed: gold pushed toward $4,200 intraday but faded into the close — spot ended ~$4,167-4,182, up ~0.2-0.6% on the day after Thursday's +1.6% close at $4,170.70. The drivers point both ways: the dollar fade and the 10-year's slide to ~5.09% are classic gold fuel (no yield to compete with), and haven flow from Hormuz/Middle East risk helped — but three hot US inflation prints in three days plus a ~90%+ priced December hike are the ceiling. Thread: morning — the anti-dollar bid held: spot closed ~$4,158-4,159 Thursday (+1.3%) and sat ~$4,172 in Asia as the 10-year fell to one-month lows. What it means: confirms. Gold is doing exactly what the framework says: up on dollar weakness and falling yields, capped by hawkish Fed pricing. Four beats on the $4,200 cap: (1) gold keeps failing near $4,200; (2) it's up ~0.9% on the week but still ~23% below January's $5,405 record; (3) the cap is arithmetic — a December hike near ~90%+ (Thursday's LSEG read; the split vs one ~67% desk read is still flagged) means real yields stay high, and gold pays nothing; (4) for FX: gold's message is the dollar's message in reverse — sustained $4,200+ needs the December hike pricing to crack.
chapters.fx: What to watch: December hike pricing — any crack lifts the cap; weekend haven headlines; $4,188 as the near-term line.
numbers: Dec Fed hike ~90%+ priced (the ceiling; split flagged)
